400.text: Health equity in cancer outcomes is the absence of disparities for people with different levels of social advantage. 1

408.text: Achieving equity requires action to empower health services, systems and communities to recognise and respond to social, cultural, commercial, and environmental determinants of health that impact access to care. 2

414.text: The Australian Cancer Plan highlights and aims to address disparities in cancer outcomes that exist between defined groups of the Australian population. 3 Intersectionality can compound inequities 4 and it is important to recognise that for many people, overlapping factors influence their cancer risk, diagnosis, treatment access and outcomes.

485.text: Services should collect and review data to understand disparities in cancer outcomes and their drivers to inform planning and delivery of equitable cancer care. 5

520.text: People working at all levels of a health service should undertake training in and maintain a sustained focus on unconscious bias and institutional racism 6 , 7 to ensure that people do not experience disparities in access or care due to: – age – gender – geography – ethnicity – sexuality – language – physical or cognitive disability – cultural or religious factors.

535.text: People working at all levels of the service should undertake training in and maintain a sustained focus on cultural competence knowledge, awareness, behaviour, skills and attitudes. 8 , 9

543.text: People receiving cancer care should be asked how they identify to enable delivery of personalised and culturally safe care. 10 How people identify must not influence the quality of care provided.

551.text: Services should be delivered with due consideration of the financial impact of cancer, its diagnosis and treatment, with information and support provided to reduce the risk and impact of financial toxicity. 11

559.text: Services delivering cancer care should utilise telehealth 12 and flexible service models to enable access to services and support appropriate to the person’s location and circumstances.

573.text: Services should apply co-design principles to ensure that services meet the needs and priorities of communities they are designed for. 13

585.text: Services delivering cancer care should have structures, services and environments appropriate to the age of people receiving care. 14 , 15 , 16

593.text: All cancer care professionals should recognise the prevalence of trauma and be sensitive to and respectful of how past or ongoing trauma may impact a person’s engagement with health services and cancer care. This extends to the person’s family, carers and community. 17

1729.text: Supportive care involves prevention and management of the adverse effects of cancer and its treatment, including management of physical and psychological symptoms and side effects across the cancer continuum. Supportive care aims to improve the quality of rehabilitation, secondary cancer prevention, survivorship, and end-of-life care. 59

1737.text: Supportive care is an essential component of cancer care that requires multidisciplinary input and interventions. It is needs based and is important for people with cancer, their families and carers. Supportive care is important across all steps of the optimal care pathway. Definitions and frameworks have evolved over time, incorporating elements of survivorship care and palliative care. 60
